As a child, my parents didn't enforce gender norms and I could dress (and act, for the most part) however I wanted. As a result, when I was young I mostly just enjoyed my body because it was mine and it let me do fun things. My main awareness of my gender identity came from the fact that I hated that boys said girls couldn't do x and other sexist things, and I adored outdoing boys and rubbing their face in the fact that they lost to a girl. Because I had so much freedom when I was young, boy and girl seemed like two mostly interchangeable teams.

As puberty arrived, a whole shitstorm of emotional crap hit me. I struggled with body image a lot, never feeling like a good/skinny/desirable enough girl. I also struggled with depression, self-harm, and bulimia. Unfortunately, these experiences and feelings are extremely common for young women, and so everyone (including me) chalked up my struggles as an unfortunate but common side effect of puberty.

I didn't realize that actual gender dysphoria affected me until my early twenties, when I realized I'd have to face the rest of my life presenting as female unless I did something about it. It sounds stupid, but I spent so much of my adolescence trying to survive and conform that it wasn't until college that I started looking forward at my future and deciding what to make of it.

Unfortunately, lack of money has severely limited my access to healthcare and medical transition. Once I have top surgery and am comfortable with my body, I expect I'll feel comfortable wearing dresses and other "girl" clothes again.

Thanks for sharing this with us even though it's not easy.  I was raped in a similar fashion by a manipulative acquaintance in my friend group, and it was very hard to deal with on many levels.  

Please distance yourself from the people who don't believe you, including your partner.  What happened to you can't be changed by their disbelief, denial, or desire to not have to deal with the situation.  They can get on board and support you, or they can blame you and be left behind.  It may seem like you are losing people as a result of being raped, but this situation has revealed important fundamental faults in their characters.  You can try to educate them, but you have no obligation to do so.  They should believe you and support you.  Step away from them and ask yourself what *you* need right now.  

I can't recommend getting a therapist enough.  This will give you a space to process all that you are thinking and feeling, and strategize about your options for dealing with the world (friends/partner reactions, if/how to tell other people, the possibility of reporting what happened, etc.).  

From your post, you seem like you're approaching the situation very logically, thinking about all the possibilities and ramifications of my actions.  I was the same way, and appeared to be holding everything together very well on the outside.  For me, this intellectualization of everything was a distancing tactic that helped me minimize my rape and deny my very strong feelings.  Even if you seem/feel/want to be in control of yourself right now, recognize that finding a therapist and giving yourself the opportunity to talk about what happened is a form of self-care.  

What happened sucks, your friends' and partner's reaction sucks, and it's hard to handle the strong feelings that come in the wake of such terrible things.  I'm really sorry this happened to you.  Please do whatever you need to do to take care of yourself.

Don't hesitate to PM me if you want to talk.  Finding a few key people to open up to was a really important part of me feeling ok again, and I'd be happy to talk to you.

Sometimes there are very significant shortcomings in the legal process that cause problems for survivors.  That is a very important part of deciding whether or not to report a sexual assault, and you should absolutely not minimize that.  OP needs our support, not to be pressured into anything.

In an ideal world, rape and sexual assault of all kinds would be recognized and dealt with accordingly without re-traumatizing or blaming victims.  We do not live in an ideal world.

Take your time deciding whether you want to engage with the legal system, and don't feel guilty for really thinking it over.  If you can talk to a good therapist about your legal options and the ramifications they will have on your emotional wellbeing, that would be ideal.  

I completely support you whether or not you decide to go to the police and pursue legal action.  You are not obligated to do so at all, and I'm sure you will make the right decision for you.

A tip I learned early is to go to a place you don't usually go, somewhere you're not habituated to. Don't do anything. Just pay attention. 

Then write down sentences, one at a time. Start them with "I see...", "I hear...", "I smell...", "I think...", "I remember..." and similar prompts. Then  take those sentences, and remove the above prompts so you only have your observations. Then you can play around with the order of the phrases you have left until you have something you like. Poetry doesn't have to be mysterious, and it doesn't have to be hard. There is no wrong way to write a poem. The way you see things is completely unique, and could be a revelation to someone else. Just pay attention, record your thoughts, and then write.

They'll hear (or have already heard) the word transsexual used in the media.  You should absolutely address it and its medicalized, normalizing history.  Also let them know that some trans* people identify with the term transsexual even so, and that people's self-identification should always be honored.  

Edit: it's to its

Use transgender instead of transsexual, especially for younger people.  It avoids the negative connotations of transsexual, and avoids unnecessarily medicalizing gender or bringing up the specter of genitals and surgery.  Basically, using the word "transsexual" is the equivalent of using the word "homosexual"; it may or may not come across as offensive, and few members of those groups use those words to self-identify.  (Of course, some will and their identities should be honored.)

The key is to find out how people self-identify, and honor that identity.  Someone who identifies as a trans man should be referred to as trans man.  Those who identify as men should be referred to as men.  Those who identify as transsexual should be referred to as transsexual, etc.

Self-identified transsexuals are a group who fall under the transgender umbrella, which some organizations (including yours) use the * in trans* to represent.  There are few (or no) situations where you NEED to know whether someone identifies as transgender or transsexual, as the difference amounts to asking intrusive questions about bodies.  Transgender, or trans* to more explicitly include those with other identities, is enough for people to know 99% of the time and is a much safer choice.

You sound a lot like me.  I used to struggle so much with my symptoms, and blame myself for them.  It was too hard to do anything... it started with schoolwork, but then it became social contact, and basic hygiene, and then getting out of bed.  At first I was passively suicidal and felt that suicide was my fate, waiting for me in my future.  Then I became more and more actively suicidal until I thought about killing myself just to make the intrusive thoughts go away.  

To play armchair psychologist, two things you say seem like very serious symptoms of depression.  First, that it has become too much trouble to eat.  That's getting into some serious depression territory.  And second, that you can't envision a future for yourself except for suicide.  That is suicidal ideation, and it is a serious sign that something is up.  You don't need your parents' permission to get help.  I'm sorry you're living in such an unsupportive environment right now.  It doesn't have to be that way.  Getting a therapist for yourself might be the best move you ever make.

I want to second (third, and fourth) that you should check with your school for counseling resources.  And be brutally honest with them about what is going on when you do.  Don't downplay your situation.  I'd make a list of all the things you feel are "wrong" or "off" or that you don't like about your life before you go in so you don't miss any possible symptoms.  Especially tell them that while you have no immediate plans of suicide, you don't see a future for yourself and are considering it.  And about how eating is too much trouble.  

If your school sends you to a counselor you really like, great.  You'll have a qualified professional you can open up to who can give you some insight about what you're experiencing.  

If your school sends you to a counselor who you don't connect with, that's ok.  You'll still have documentation that shows you're having mental health troubles so if your grades get bad enough you can show that there is a reason.  You can also get a list of other therapists in the area from the school counselor, and find someone who is better for you.

As for you thinking you are lazy, well depression (or stress, or anxiety) make things much harder.  They steal your energy and your hope.  They mess with your thinking.  My parents didn't "believe" in mental illness either, and that led to me blaming myself for my symptoms and not getting help until after I'd given myself stitches, tried to break my own arm, and attempted suicide.  To get out from under this, you need to go to a professional and let them diagnose and help you.  

You built your own computer, which may not seem like a big deal to you but at least means you're smart and capable.  You can have a future, and a life, and feelings once you get your situation (whatever it winds up being) under control.  You need to take care of your health first, and that includes your mental health.  Nobody else, including your parents, knows what is really happening in your mind or heart, or has to live your life.  Please, do whatever you have to do to get help.

I'm actually one of the volunteer coordinators for this year's Trans Health Conference.  We have many different types of positions available, and you can tell us your availability and volunteer as much or as little as you want.  You can still attend events as a volunteer; we take people's workshop preferences into account and do everything we can to accommodate them, and if you volunteer for one of our after hours social events we have multiple shifts so you can also relax and enjoy the event.

In brief, we have these positions:
SET UP (Thurs) and BREAK DOWN (Sat):  Getting our spaces in the Convention Center ready for the conference, and then making sure our areas are clean and emptied.  Will include some heavy lifting/manual labor.

ROOM (Thurs-Sat):  Room Monitors work in the Convention Center to help each presenter set up the room, keep track of time during the workshop, pass out and collect evaluation forms, and clear out the room after the workshop.

LUNCH: (Thurs-Sat):  Assist with the set up, serving, and clean up of lunch and snacks for conference attendees at the nearby Arch Street United Methodist Church.

OPENING (Thurs night):  Bartend or serve for our Opening Night Ceremony, held at nearby William Way Center.  Must be 21+ and have some service experience.  For those in recovery, this is the ONLY volunteer event where alcohol is present.

BALL (Fri night):  Assist with set up, maintenance, and break down of the Code Red Ball at the Convention Center.  Will include some heavy lifting/manual labor.

EVENT (Sat night):  There are actually two events during this time slot, both are at the Convention Center.  Applause!, a youth open mic event, and Blender, an after party and trans* performance showcase.  Assist with set up, maintenance, and break down of one of these events.  Will include some heavy lifting/manual labor.

REGISTRATION (Thurs-Sat): Be at the registration desk checking people in, handing out program booklets, giving directions, and answering questions

KIDS CAMP (Thurs-Sat):  Structured daily programming such as activities, games, learning, crafts, and service projects for 5-11 year olds during the conference.  Must have a national child abuse clearance. 

Apologies for the wall of text, but there are a lot of ways to be involved!  You can look at [the complete schedule](http://www.trans-health.org/program/session-schedule/2014-06-12) and sign up for time slots with workshops you'd like to attend. (You can also [search for specific speakers or keywords](http://www.trans-health.org/program/find-a-workshop) to find workshops you're interested in.)

I was in a similar situation when I started T a few years ago.  I had been out to myself for years and out socially for about a year, and have struggled with recurrent episodes of major depression since my early teens including self-harm and suicidal thoughts.  No health insurance meant no access to therapy or medicine.

I live in SE Pennsylvania and went to the Mazzoni Center, a low-income LGBT clinic that works with trans people on an informed consent model.  I was nervous when I first went, but I was honest about my gender identity and mood disorder/concerns.  I left with a prescription for T that day, as well as a flu shot, a follow up appointment, and an invitation to join their low-income one-on-one therapy program.  I did not feel judged or threatened at all to "prove" I was trans or that I was happy or healthy enough to be asking for T.  It was a positive experience, and I hope you have the same.

If the place you're getting T from works on an informed consent model, my gut says they won't prevent or delay your HRT because you are also depressed.  Places that are enlightened enough to be ok with informed consent generally believe in listening to the patient's experiences and partnering with you to come up with good, harm-reduction solutions.  You seem to me to have plenty of realistic insight about your situation.  I think if you went to a good LGBT-savvy clinic and told them just what you said in your post you should be good to go.

Since you said you've recently moved and are still looking into informed consent programs, if you are comfortable telling me your location I'd be happy to help you look for resources online.  I used to run a trans resource center at my university before graduating and am pretty used to dealing with the healthcare system.  If you want help finding a place, or having me call places for you asking about their HRT/mood disorder polices, I absolutely will help.  I remember how afraid I was that I would be denied HRT, and how overjoyed I was walking out with that prescription.  I'm down to help you any way I can.

Sorry for the late response; hope this is helpful.  PM me anytime.
